turns.text: Hi Meera, good to start the week with you. What stood out today?

So today was mostly about the ledger reconciliation job. It's been slow for a while, the nightly run takes about 50 minutes now, and I spent the day profiling it. I found that it does an N+1 query pattern, it fetches each journal entry's account one by one.
That sounds like a solid find. What do you plan to do about the N+1 pattern?

I'll batch the account lookups and probably add an index on the entries table. Also, the design doc for the webhook retry service got approved today. We went with exponential backoff with jitter and a dead-letter queue after eight attempts, and I wrote most of that doc.
Nice. What was the hardest part of getting the design approved?
Honestly the debate about whether retries should live in the API or in a separate worker. I argued for a separate worker so a slow merchant endpoint can't block anything else, and the team agreed.
And what's the one thing for tomorrow?
Tomorrow I want to start building the retry worker skeleton.

turns.text: Yesterday you planned to start the retry worker skeleton. How did it go?

Pretty good. I got the skeleton running locally. It picks failed deliveries from a Postgres table using SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so multiple workers don't grab the same webhook. I hadn't used SKIP LOCKED before, so that was a nice thing to learn.
What else happened today?

I also started mentoring the new intern on our team. I helped them set up the local environment, and we paired for about an hour on their first pull request, which was a small fix in the ledger API's pagination.
How did the pairing go for them?
They were nervous at first, but by the end they were driving and asking good questions about why we use cursor pagination. I think it helped them feel less lost.
Anything that felt hard today?
Not really, it was a calm day. Mostly heads down.

turns.text: Hi Meera. Before we start, one from yesterday: did the intern's pull request get merged?
Yes, it got merged this morning, they were really happy about it.
Great. What stood out today?
Two things. The good one is the ledger. I batched the account lookups and added a composite index on journal entries, and the main reconciliation query went from 900 milliseconds to 120 milliseconds.
That's a big drop. And the other thing?

The other thing is a blocker. The settlement events consumer on Kafka is lagging badly, the lag is at about 2 million messages and it keeps growing. Settlements are landing in the ledger hours late, and I couldn't figure out why today.
That sounds stressful. What have you ruled out so far?
It's not the broker, the brokers look healthy. I think the consumer group keeps rebalancing, but I need to dig into the logs tomorrow.

turns.text: Hi Meera. How are you doing today?
Tired. I was on call last night and got paged at 2 am. The payout webhooks were failing with 500 errors, and it turned out the database connection pool was exhausted.
That's a rough night. What did you do once you saw the pool was exhausted?

I traced it to a batch export job that was leaking connections, it never returned them to the pool. I killed the job, rolled back the deploy that introduced it, and payouts were flowing again in about 40 minutes. I was alone on it until my lead joined around 3.
How did it end?
It ended well actually. No payouts were lost, everything that failed got retried, and by morning the queue was clear. I was shaky but I'm kind of proud of how calm I stayed.
What did you learn from the night?
That our runbook for connection pool alerts was useless. It just said check the database. I want to write a proper postmortem tomorrow and fix the runbook.

turns.text: Hi Meera. Go ahead and tell me everything about today, I'll ask follow-ups after.

Okay so, I wrote the postmortem for Wednesday night's incident and rewrote the connection pool runbook with actual steps, like how to find which job is holding connections. My lead shared the postmortem in the engineering channel and said it was one of the clearest incident write-ups they'd read, and that the way I handled the night was exactly what on-call should look like. That felt really good. On the Kafka thing, I found the cause, the consumer takes too long per batch so it blows past max poll interval, and the group rebalances, and every rebalance makes the lag worse. I haven't fixed it yet though.
Thanks, that's a full day. What's your plan for the Kafka fix?
I'm going to try the cooperative sticky assignor and smaller batches, and commit offsets per batch. I'll test it on staging Monday.
Sounds good. Is there anything else from today?
No, that's it. Happy it's Friday.

turns.text: Last Friday you planned to test the Kafka fix on staging. How did it go?

It worked! I switched the settlement consumer to the cooperative sticky assignor, made the batches smaller and commit offsets after each batch. On staging the rebalances stopped, so I rolled it to production in the afternoon. The lag went from about 2 million messages to under 5,000 within two hours.
That's a huge drop. What was your part versus the team's?
That was me, I did the fix and the rollout. The platform team just reviewed the config change.
Nice work. Anything else today?

I reviewed the intern's design for a CSV export of ledger statements. I didn't give them the answer, I asked questions until they found the memory problem with loading everything at once themselves, and they switched to streaming rows. They told me it was the first time a review felt like learning instead of being corrected.
What's the one thing for tomorrow?
Tomorrow is the big one, the ledger entries migration to partitioned tables.

turns.text: Yesterday you said today was the ledger entries migration. How did it go?

It went really well. We moved the journal entries table to monthly partitions, about 18 million rows, with zero downtime. I wrote the migration plan and ran the backfill in chunks with a dual write in between.
What changed after the migration?
The nightly reconciliation got 50% faster, because it only scans the current month's partition now.
Was this something you led or a team effort?
I led it. One teammate helped with the dual write code, and I owned the plan, the backfill and the cutover.
What did you learn along the way?
That Postgres partition pruning only kicks in if the query filters on the partition key directly. I had to rewrite two reconciliation queries so the planner could prune.

You owned the plan, the chunked backfill and the cutover, with a teammate helping on the dual writes. You said nightly reconciliation got 50% faster because it now scans only the current month. You learned that partition pruning needs queries to filter on the partition key directly.

turns.text: Hi Meera. What stood out today?
We shipped the webhook retry service to 100% of merchants today. Failed webhook deliveries dropped from about 1,200 a day to under 100 a day.
That's a big change. How did you roll it out?
Gradually. Five percent of merchants first, then 25, then everyone today, with a kill switch flag the whole time. I built the worker and the dead-letter queue, and I ran the rollout.
What was the hard part?
A couple of merchants have endpoints that time out after two seconds, so I had to make the timeout configurable per merchant. That took most of yesterday afternoon.
Anything else from today?
I also helped a teammate set up the Grafana dashboard for retry attempts, mostly by pointing them at the right metrics.

days.day_summary: You shipped the webhook retry service to all merchants, and failed webhook deliveries dropped from about 1,200 a day to under 100. You built the worker and the dead-letter queue and ran a gradual rollout behind a kill switch. The hard part was merchants whose endpoints time out quickly, which you solved with per-merchant timeouts. You also helped a teammate set up a Grafana dashboard for retry attempts.

turns.text: Yesterday you planned to start the load test for the retry service. How did it go?

Halfway. I wrote the k6 scripts and ran it up to 300 requests per second, and it held fine. Past that the dead-letter queue writes start slowing down, but I ran out of time before finding the ceiling.
What else happened today?
I tuned the alert thresholds for the retry service, they were paging on every single merchant timeout. The alerts are way quieter now, but I don't have the exact numbers in front of me.
That's fine, I can ask you next time. Anything else?
The team finished rolling out idempotency keys on the ledger API write endpoints. I reviewed some of the PRs, but I'm not sure how much of that counts as mine.
Okay. What's the one thing for next time?
Finish the load test for the retry service and find where it actually breaks.
